title: Tesla Stock Faces 3 Tests as China Retail Sales Fall 66.1%
summary: Tesla stock faces three tests as China domestic sales fell 66.1% in October, legal exposure stays unsettled and the Cybercab must prove its economics.
body_markdown:
October 2026 (CPCA data via CnEVPost) Vehicles Change vs. October 2025


Tesla China domestic retail sales 8,817 -66.1%


Tesla Shanghai exports 59,012 +66.27%


Tesla China wholesale, exports included 67,829 +10.3%


China passenger BEV retail market 770,000 -5.3%


Over the first 10 months of 2026, Tesla's China retail sales fell 15% to 389,905 vehicles, while Shanghai exports rose 101.28% to 420,984, according to CnEVPost. The Motley Fool cautioned against reading too much into October alone, since Tesla usually pushes exports early in a quarter. Its larger point is that exports are an outlet, not an escape from competition: BYD's overseas shipments jumped roughly 103% in October, the article said, as the Chinese automaker offset weak demand and a price war at home.


## Electrek Puts Tesla Legal Exposure at $2.7 Billion to $14.5 Billion


The second challenge is the courtroom. The Motley Fool cited an April analysis by Electrek that put Tesla's potential exposure across lawsuits and regulatory matters at $2.7 billion to $14.5 billion, stressing that the range is an outside estimate, not an amount Tesla owes, has reserved or expects to pay.


The article's clearest example is the Benavides Autopilot case, in which a jury awarded $129 million in compensatory damages, assigning Tesla 33% of the fault, plus $200 million in punitive damages. Per The Motley Fool, Tesla's portion works out to approximately $243 million, and the company is appealing, according to its latest[quarterly report](https://www.heygotrade.com/en/learn/how-to-read-an-earnings-report/) .


The same filing disclosed that an appeals court vacated class certification in a separate driver-assistance advertising case in October, sending it back to the lower court. Tesla says it cannot reasonably estimate potential losses in these matters, and The Motley Fool framed that uncertainty as the real problem for now.


## Cybertruck Wind-Down Around Mid-2027 Makes Room for Cybercab


Elon Musk wrote on X that "Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,"[Fox Business](https://www.foxbusiness.com/markets/tesla-wind-down-cybertruck-production-texas-factory-next-year-make-room-cybercab) reported on Nov. 6. Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and said the move marks the "end of an era."


The pickup fell well short of early targets. Citing Kelley Blue Book, Fox Business reported that Tesla sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the U.S. in 2025, a 48% decline from 38,965 in 2024, after Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units when production started in 2023.


The Cybercab, a two-seat robotaxi, entered production in 2026, and Tesla has listed an installed capacity of more than 125,000 units, according to Fox Business. Tesla began paid Cybercab rides in Austin in September, and about 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis operating in Texas are Cybercabs, the outlet reported, citing the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles. Tesla said on Nov. 19 that it had[launched its Cybercab robotaxi in Dallas](https://www.heygotrade.com/en/news/tesla-tsla-stock-news-november-20-2026/) .


Regulators are watching as well. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit in September to review whether Tesla properly self-certified the Cybercab under federal motor vehicle safety standards, Fox Business reported, and The Motley Fool noted that the inquiry is not a finding of wrongdoing. The article added that building more Cybercabs is not the same as running a profitable robotaxi business.


> "Tesla needs enough paying rides to cover vehicles, charging, maintenance, insurance, and fleet operations."
>
>
> Daniel Miller, The Motley Fool
